issues.description: Regex name HAS_TIME is slightly misleading for the shape it matches
issues.detail: The regex `/\dm?s/i` matches a digit followed by optional 'm' and an 's' — it's a cheap prefilter for 'looks like it might contain a time token,' not a true 'has time' predicate. Values like 'foo1s' or '1sigma' would pass. That's fine as a fast-path gate before the real parser runs, but the name oversells what the data actually says. A name like `MAYBE_HAS_TIME` or a one-line comment ('cheap prefilter; real parsing happens below') would make the data flow self-evident.

issues.description: Same prefilter pattern likely belongs as a shared helper if other time-rules need it
issues.detail: This is exactly the Unix-filter shape: cheap stateless test on the input string, short-circuit before expensive parsing. If issue #6869 covers other time-related rules (it's a perf umbrella), the same prefilter will reappear. Worth noting — not blocking — that a single exported predicate (e.g., `hasTimeToken(value)`) composed by each rule beats copy-paste regexes drifting apart. Leave it inline for now; promote on the second copy.

review.summary: SMALL-AND-COMPOSABLE. This is the right shape of fix: a cheap stateless prefilter on the declaration value runs before the expensive `valueParser` + `vendor.unprefixed` work, and the unprefix call is also moved past the early-return so it only pays cost when the value plausibly contains a time. That's measurement-driven optimization applied to the obvious bottleneck — `walkDecls` runs on every declaration, and most declarations have no time token. The data structure (the raw value string) is being interrogated in the cheapest possible way before any AST is built. Two minor notes: the regex name `HAS_TIME` overstates what `/\\dm?s/i` actually proves (it's a prefilter, not a predicate), and the same shape will probably want to be shared if other time-rules adopt it — but neither blocks the merge. Changeset and scope are appropriate.
